description: I'm a developer and space enthusiast focused on turning NASA open data into an intuitive, high-impact application. I'm handling the core technical build and looking for teammates with skills in science communication, education, data visualization, or presentation storytelling to round out the team and make our project stand out.
summary: SELENE is a web app that scores hexagonal cells of the lunar south pole (80°S to 90°S) on five criteria: sunlight, communications with Earth, terrain safety, proximity to water ice, and shielding. No site is best at all five, so the app lets the user set the weight of each criterion, apply hard limits, and see every cell rescored on the map at once. One-click presets cover three mission types (an Artemis IV crewed sortie, a CLPS ice-prospecting rover and a permanent Base Camp). For any cell, the inspector draws the full local skyline from a detailed elevation map with the paths of the Sun and the Earth, which shows when and why the site is lit, dark or out of contact. Up to three candidate cells can be pinned and compared side by side. All values come from NASA data (LRO LOLA elevation, LRO Diviner temperatures, JPL Horizons ephemeris), processed offline and served as static files, so the app runs in any browser with no server. It addresses the "Lunar Landing Site Navigator" challenge by turning public NASA datasets into a tool that mission planners, students and the public can use to explore the trade-offs of landing and living at the south pole.
details:
Detailed Project Description

What it does

  • Shows a polar stereographic map of the lunar south pole over LOLA shaded relief, divided into 14,444 hexagonal cells (H3 resolution 5), with a finer patch of 6,024 cells over Shackleton crater and its ridge that appears on zoom.
  • Scores every cell from 0 to 1 with a multi-criteria decision analysis over five criteria: sunlight, Earth communications, terrain safety, ice proximity and shielding. The user moves the weight sliders and sets hard filters (maximum slope, longest darkness, minimum Earth visibility, minimum safe-slope fraction); the map and a top-10 list update at once.
  • Offers three mission presets: Artemis IV (crewed sortie), CLPS (ice-prospecting rover) and Base Camp (permanent habitat). The preset weights are our own assumptions.
  • Lets the user choose what the map colours show: the overall score or any single measurement (sunlight, slope, temperature, ice index and others), through the "Colour by" selector in the legend.
  • Inspects any cell: its measured values with units, and a 360° chart of the terrain horizon with the paths of the Sun and the Earth over the selected dates.
  • Gives mission tools for the selected cell: distance and steepest slope to the nearest ice-bearing cell, and a first-order battery mass estimate for the longest night.
  • Compares up to three pinned cells side by side, highlighting the best value in each row.
  • Recomputes sunlight and Earth visibility in the browser for a date range chosen by the user, with one-click polar summer and polar winter months, and shows when NASA Deep Space Network stations (Madrid, Goldstone, Canberra) can see the Moon. The baseline analysis covers the year 2027.
  • Includes its own documentation: a technical primer with the formulas, an outreach guide and a validation report.

How it works

  1. An offline Python pipeline reads the NASA elevation models, temperature maps and ephemeris. For each cell it traces 360 horizon rays out to 150 km over the true lunar sphere, measures slope and roughness, evaluates ice stability, and computes hourly sunlight (Sun treated as a disc) and Earth visibility for the whole of 2027.
  2. The results are written as compact static files checked against a schema: cell measurements, horizon tables, the ephemeris table and a shaded-relief basemap (about 25 MB).
  3. A static web app loads those files and does everything else in the browser: scoring, colouring, the horizon chart, and the date-range recomputation in a background worker.

Validation

Our one-year sunlight map was compared with NASA's published multi-year LOLA illumination map: correlation 0.992, mean difference 0.4 percentage points. Earth visibility: correlation 0.988, about 4 points lower than NASA's map, as expected because NASA's map counts any visible part of Earth's disc.

Benefits

  • Makes the trade-offs between sunlight, ice, communications and terrain visible and adjustable, instead of giving one fixed ranking.
  • Explains each value: the horizon chart shows the cause of darkness or loss of contact at a site.
  • Runs anywhere as a static site, with no server or login.

Limits of the current version

  • Slopes are measured on the 80 m elevation model. Temperatures come from the Diviner Polar Resource Product, a thermal model at about 500 m resolution.
  • Only the south polar cap is covered, and only the Shackleton detail patch is built.
  • The battery estimate and the mission preset weights are indicative.

Future vision

Detail patches for the Malapert massif and Cabeus crater; least-cost traverse routes between a base and the ice; any lunar region, with the Apollo sites for comparison; sunlight over the full 18.6-year lunar cycle; more ground-station networks; a Spanish interface.

Tools, languages and software

  • Pipeline: Python 3.12, NumPy, Numba, Rasterio, h3, Pillow, jsonschema; pytest and Ruff for checks.
  • Web app: TypeScript, React, deck.gl, h3-js, Apache ECharts, astronomy-engine, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, react-markdown with KaTeX, Vite; Vitest, Playwright and ESLint for checks.
  • Hardware: a 2-core development server (the full 2027 build takes about 24 minutes).

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) / AI

AI tools were used to speed up execution, under the team's direction and review:

  • Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code: wrote most of the pipeline and web app code, the automated tests and parts of the documentation, working from the team's plan and decisions. It also drafted the slide deck and the text of this project page.
  • Gemini (Google): used for preparatory research on the challenge, drafts of the documentation and second-opinion reads of the code.

AI-generated code and text are acknowledged here and in the repository. The SELENE emblem shown in the app and the README is an AI-generated image and carries a visible "AI-generated image" watermark. Every other image in the app and in the slides is a screenshot of the working app or is derived from NASA data. There is no AI-generated video or audio. No NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers are used.
